title: Why I spent 5 years+ building a custom Trading DSL & Voice AI Assistant (TDSL + Inspector AI) instead of using Python/MQL/Pine
author: ask4abusaidu

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The hard part of “compile once, use everywhere” seems less like TDSL code generation and more like preserving execution semantics. How do you handle a strategy whose assumptions differ between cTrader Open API, MT5, and Binance/Bybit, for example hedging versus netting, partial fills, tick sizes, or unavailable order types? I’d build a conformance suite that sends identical TDSL scenarios through each adapter and compares resulting orders, fills, positions, and rejection states. It would also clarify whether Inspector AI can merely inspect and orchestrate approved strategies or alter executable parameters by voice.

replies.author: ask4abusaidu
replies.body:
This is the real problem, and you've described it better than I did in the post.



How it works now:



Hedging vs netting: \[e.g., each adapter declares its position model; a strategy that needs hedging fails at compile/deploy time on a netting venue instead of silently behaving differently\]

Order types: \[e.g., unsupported types are rejected up front / emulated client-side, flagged as emulated\]

Tick size / lot step: \[e.g., normalized per symbol from the venue's spec before sending\]

Partial fills: \[how they're surfaced to the strategy\]

Your conformance suite idea is exactly right. \[We have something like it for X / it's not built yet and this is pushing it up the list.\] Same TDSL scenario through every adapter, then diff orders, fills, positions, and rejects.



On Inspector AI: \[it can only inspect and orchestrate approved strategies; any change to executable parameters needs explicit confirmation / it can't change parameters at all\]. Changing a live strategy by voice without a confirmation step would be a bad idea.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: five years on a DSL is real commitment. the hard part with compile once, use everywhere tends to be the fills, not the syntax: the same rule on cTrader and on a broker with wider spreads gives two different results. does the backtest model each broker's costs separately?

replies.author: ask4abusaidu
replies.body:
Fair point. The syntax is the easy part, fills are where portability breaks.



Right now the backtester \[uses a per-broker cost profile: spread, commission, swap, and slippage per symbol / uses one global cost model you set per run\]. \[If per-broker:\] So the same rule run against a cTrader feed and a wider-spread broker gives different results, and you're meant to see that before going live. \[If not yet:\] Per-broker cost profiles are next on the list, because you're right that one global model hides exactly the gap you're describing.



Curious how you handle it today. Do you calibrate slippage from your own live fills, or use a fixed assumption?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: From live fills where I can: log the expected price against the actual fill for every order, split by entry versus stop exits, by session and by news windows, and use a high percentile (say the 80th to 90th) as the tester's slippage instead of the average. Where there's no live data yet, a padded estimate scaled to the bar's range or ATR works as a starting point, as long as it's labelled as an assumption and replaced once real fills exist. Wiring each broker's commission and swap into the tester is the right next step, since the same rule really does differ across brokers.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Building a language and an engine from scratch for five years is a serious effort, and the voice assistant is the part that needs the most care. I'd check three things. First, indicator parity: run the same indicators on the same candles in TDSL, MT5 and a reference library, and publish the differences, since small formula differences (smoothing, warm-up) change signals. Second, the permissions of the AI: in the screenshot the assistant comments on large open drawdowns, so I'd keep it read-only by default, with any order or stop changes needing a separate confirmation and hard limits for size and loss enforced outside the model. Third, the tester's fill assumptions (spread, slippage, commission per broker) and a held-out period, so users can trust the backtest before connecting a live account. Bring Your Own Agent at Cymetica is one place to see how agents are connected to markets with limits set outside the model.
